LEARNING PATH LESSON · MATCHING & SORTING · AGES 2 YEARS

Match Triangle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson closes the shape-matching run with the pointiest card in the deck: one triangle above, its twin hiding below, and three corners to count on the way.

What is this?

A triangle is the shape with three straight sides and three sharp corners — the one that looks like a roof or a mountain. Among softer shapes, those points shine out.

What does it mean?

Counting the corners gives the match a handle a two-year-old can grip: one, two, three taps on the points. Numbers and shapes meet on this card, and both get stronger.

What does the child need to know?

The trace-and-count trip is the real work: side, corner, side, corner. Whether the count lands on two or three matters less than the pointing finger keeping its own rhythm.

Why this matters

Triangles hide in plain sight — roofs, sandwiches cut corner to corner, mountains in books, ramps of toy tracks. Once named, they get spotted everywhere by proud new eyes.

What it teaches

Shape matching with counting woven in, corner-spotting, and finger tracing with stops — the precise finger control that later steadies a pencil.

Words to learn

trianglethreecornerssidesmatchpointy

Say this to your child

“"A triangle! One, two, three corners — tap, tap, tap. Can you find the triangle below? Trace the sides… tap each point… there! Triangle and triangle — they match."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and trace the triangle slowly, stopping hard at each corner with a tap: one, two, three!
  2. Say the shape’s story simply: three sides, three corners, very pointy. Let your finger do the proving.
  3. Tour the row below together, tapping corners where they appear, until the twin triangle turns up — then trace both, corner to corner.
  4. Count the corners on your toddler’s fingers too: three corners, three fingers held up. The number and the shape now share a home.
  5. End with a real find: a triangle slice of toast, a roof out the window, a pointy mountain in a book — traced, tapped and counted once each.

Look closer at the picture

The card shows a triangle matching activity with basic shape choices — one triangle to match, other shapes beside it. Ask your toddler to tap each corner of the big triangle, then hunt the row for the shape with three points.

Ask your child

"How many corners?" "Where is the other triangle?" "Can you tap the points?" "Can you see a triangle out the window?"

What your child can say or do

Corner-taps with a counting voice — boo, doo, free or otherwise — are a complete answer. A toddler who holds up three wobbly fingers is ahead of the lesson; a toddler who just taps the points is right on it.

Out in the real world

Lunchtime supplies triangles free of charge: toast and sandwiches cut corner to corner, pizza by the slice. Tap the corners, count them, then eat the lesson — the best cards are edible.

Try it together

Corner hunt: walk one room together tapping every pointy corner you are allowed to touch — book corners, box corners, cushion corners. Three taps per corner, then find the shape that has exactly that many.

Understanding check

Ask cold tomorrow: where is the triangle? A point straight to the points passes. If the circle gets picked first, go back to the corner-tap together — the count always settles the argument.

Parent tips

Tap the corners louder than you say the words: the beat is what makes three memorable. Save this card for after the circle lesson — corners are easier to spot once round is known.

Staying safe

Pointy-hunt rules: cards and toast corners, not table corners or sharp edges — grown-up fingers check each target first. Sitting games stay on the floor, away from busy doorways.

This lesson pairs with the Match Triangle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Matching & Sorting (Toddler 4).
